Entrevista de Jim Casper_

[](javascript:;)

L’Artiere Edizioni: Los fotolibros como objetos de arte coleccionables

Gianluca Gamberini, de L’Artiere Edizioni, habla sobre la colaboración, la experimentación y la magia de transformar un conjunto de fotografías en un libro con vida propia.

![Image 5: LArtiere Edizioni LArtiere Edizioni](https://www.lensculture.com/l-artiere-edizioni)

L’Artiere Edizioni es una editorial de fotolibros con sede en Bolonia, Italia. Fue fundada en 2013 por los hermanos gemelos Gianluca y Gianmarco Gamberini. Provenientes de disciplinas diferentes y complementarias (Gianluca hizo cine durante 10 años y Gianmarco tiene experiencia en producción), decidieron unir fuerzas en torno a un medio artístico que a ambos les fascinaba: los fotolibros.

Comenzaron su andadura cuando su amigo Larry Fink los animó a publicar la versión europea de su libro \The Beat\_. Empezaron a desarrollar una serie de fotolibros y Larry les presentó a la fotógrafa Andrea Modica, cuya obra continúan publicando hoy en día. Tras un par de años aprendiendo el negocio de la edición y la distribución, se adentraron de manera constante en direcciones cada vez más experimentales y conceptuales para el diseño de sus libros. Hoy en día, l’Artiere goza de gran prestigio en todo como creadora de libros que son, en sí mismos, obras de arte coleccionables.

Nos complace enormemente que Gianluca haya aceptado formar parte del jurado del primer Premio de Fotolibros de LensCulture. Conversó con Jim Casper de LensCulture para esta entrevista, la cual ha sido editada._

Jim Casper: Hola, Gianluca. Estamos muy entusiasmados con este nuevo Premio de Fotolibros y verdaderamente agradecidos de que vayas a formar parte del jurado. Sois conocidos por crear fotolibros muy singulares. ¿Podrías contarme un poco cómo empezasteis y cómo describirías vuestra compañía a quienes aún no la conocen?

Gianluca Gamberini: Es un honor. Muchas gracias.

Creo que en nuestro ADN hay una gran inclinación hacia las ideas experimentales.

Tras nuestros primeros dos años publicando excelentes libros tradicionales, realmente queríamos hacer algo que se alineara más con nuestra concepción del fotolibro. Con el libro de Larry y obras como nuestro primer proyecto con Andrea Modica, tuvimos la oportunidad de empezar a comprender el mercado y establecer contactos con otras figuras del mundo editorial. Fue increíble, pero también un poco limitado.

Doble página de The Beats de Larry Fink. Cortesía de L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Así que Gianmarco y a mí nos encantó el trabajo de Amy Friend, *Stardust*. Ese año ganó el premio Photolucida. Al ver su obra dijimos: “Vaya, creo que podríamos hacer algo diferente, algo único, a medio camino entre un libro de artista y una obra dirigida a un público más amplio”.

De este modo, junto con Gianmarco, concebimos la idea de plasmar en un libro su enfoque físico al trabajar con imágenes de archivo. Utilizamos un láser para recrear las perforaciones en la página. Luego, combinando una encuadernación francesa con un papel muy fino (similar al papel biblia), al pasar la página se produce la sensación de que la luz la atraviesa. En ese momento pensamos: “¡De acuerdo! Esto es exactamente lo que nos gusta de un libro”.

A partir de entonces, siempre hemos intentado tratar cada libro como si fuera único. Trabajamos con diferentes diseñadores. Cada vez que decidimos colaborar con un fotógrafo, intentamos determinar qué diseñador resulta ser la opción más adecuada. Después, junto con el diseñador, desarrollamos una idea o concepto y, poco a poco, vamos dando forma al libro.

Cubierta desplegable para un libro de Hitoshi Fugo. Cortesía de L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Da la impresión de que hacéis algo que os apasiona profundamente y que también os aporta una gran felicidad a nivel personal.

Mucho, muchísimo. Aunque creo que cualquier editor comparte ese sentimiento; de lo contrario, probablemente nos dedicaríamos a otra cosa.

Sí. Cuéntame, ¿qué tipo de obra encaja especialmente bien con L’Artiere?

Creo que a veces resulta difícil de definir, pero básicamente tiene que enamorarnos. Debe transmitir un fuerte sentido de empatía, sin duda. Necesitamos sentir esa empatía a través de la imagen. A veces noto que también estamos muy vinculados a historias sobre la familia o la comunidad. No siempre, pero desde luego es muy común. Nos encantan los proyectos a largo plazo, aunque no siempre se pueda aplicar ese criterio a todos los libros. Y, al final, también necesitamos ser capaces de vender el libro al público; es una consideración importante.

Doble página de Napoli de Anders Petersen. Cortesía de L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Tras 13 años, ¿sientes que ya sabes cuándo un libro va a venderse bien? ¿Te sientes bastante seguro?

Gianmarco es mejor que yo. Yo siempre soy optimista, pero debo admitir que él tiene mejor ojo para predecirlo. Sin embargo, lo decidimos 50-50. Es una democracia, así que lo intentamos.

Parece que está dando buenos resultados. Para el Premio de Fotolibros de LensCulture, pedimos a los fotógrafos que presenten entre 20 y 30 imágenes y un breve texto conceptual. ¿Es suficiente para ti, como editor, para calibrar si un proyecto funcionaría como libro?

Creo que es suficiente para comprenderlo o, al menos, para decir: “Vaya, quiero ver más. Quiero saber más”. Es un buen punto de partida. A veces, cuando recibo una propuesta, les pido a los fotógrafos que me envíen un PDF con su propia idea de secuencia. Incluso si terminamos haciendo algo completamente diferente, al menos así podemos percibir una intención. En ocasiones también les pregunto si ya tienen una maqueta y que me manden un vídeo de la misma —de nuevo, aunque vayamos a hacer algo distinto—. Al menos así puedo ver algo, una intención detrás. Pero creo que 20 imágenes son más que suficientes. También debemos evaluar si la obra resulta adecuada para un público más amplio, y 20 imágenes son fantásticas para eso.

¿Y qué importancia tiene la escritura para vosotros? Un texto conceptual, un título, pies de foto, ensayos... ¿Es una parte importante de vuestros libros o dirías que están más orientados hacia la imagen y el objeto?

Pienso que es fundamental que un fotógrafo sepa escribir sobre su obra. Siempre le pido a cada fotógrafo que redacte un breve texto sobre su trabajo. Quizá no lo publiquemos, pero considero muy importante tenerlo, tanto para ellos como para nosotros, con el fin de comprender mejor la obra. Solemos prescindir de textos curatoriales. Si tengo que añadir algo, prefiero incluir cuatro o cinco líneas del fotógrafo al final, en el colofón, expresadas con sus propias palabras. Son fotógrafos, no escritores; nadie busca ganar un Premio Nobel. Pero creo que ese es el texto más importante que puede contener un fotolibro, en caso de ser necesario. Y, por supuesto, algunas obras están tan unidas a la palabra escrita que resulta indispensable combinar la imagen con el texto.

Tragedia. Fotografía de Nicola Lo Calzo. Cortesía de L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Cuéntame cómo dais a conocer vuestros libros en el mundo.

Las ferias de fotografía son lo mejor para nosotros, a pesar de que implican muchísimo trabajo. Una feria ofrece una manera fantástica de mostrar tu libro porque, al final, todos producimos objetos físicos que solo se pueden apreciar en persona. Es una forma increíble de conocer a tu público. Y luego, por supuesto, como editorial independiente, vendemos mucho a través de nuestra tienda online. Además, nuestros héroes son las librerías, especialmente las librerías especializadas de todo el mundo. En Europa creo que contamos con un poco más de librerías fotográficas verdaderamente independientes, aunque en Estados Unidos también las hay. Son nuestro principal objetivo a la hora de comercializar nuestros libros. Contamos con varios distribuidores: uno en Estados Unidos, otro en Europa y uno pequeño en Japón, los cuales nos ayudan a vender ejemplares a un público más amplio.

Nuestros libros son objetos que se vuelven cada vez más elaborados y preciosos, y las tiradas no son tan grandes, de modo que al final quienes compran y venden nuestros libros sienten una auténtica pasión por ellos.

¿Qué puede hacer un fotolibro que una exposición, un sitio web o un reportaje en una revista no puedan lograr? ¿Qué lo hace diferente?

Vengo del mundo del cine, así que esta es una muy buena pregunta. Una exposición ocurre en un momento determinado en el tiempo. Creas algo en una pared, pero también dejas mucha libertad a la gente para que interprete la narrativa. Sin embargo, en un libro hay una línea y hay una narración. Para mí, se asemeja mucho más a la idea de una película. Además, un libro perdura durante mucho tiempo. Un libro no necesita electricidad para encenderse. Lo mágico de un libro es que, cuando lo produces y lo publicas, adquiere su propia vida; nunca sabes quién entrará en contacto con él ni cuántas personas se lo pasarán unas a otras. Eso es algo bastante mágico, la verdad.

Sí, la palabra adecuada es magia. Tengo libros favoritos que siento como amigos. Puedo sacarlos de la estantería y de repente me encuentro en un espacio muy feliz. Es algo verdaderamente hermoso.

Exactamente, ese espacio de felicidad. Creo que cuando no te sientes demasiado bien, simplemente pasas un rato con algunos fotolibros y, aunque los temas no sean precisamente los más alegres, de algún modo te devuelven la esperanza.

Portada de Catholic Girls de Andrea Modica. Cortesía de L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

¿Podrías dar algún consejo a los fotógrafos que desean hacer un fotolibro?

En primer lugar, investigar a fondo. Existen muchos editores diferentes. Es un momento fantástico para los editores de fotolibros; hay una gran diversidad y cada uno de nosotros posee sus propias particularidades. Sé que resulta difícil para un fotógrafo ser totalmente objetivo al respecto

L’Artiere Edizioni: Photobooks as Collectible Art Objects

L’Artiere Edizioni’s Gianluca Gamberini talks about collaboration, experimentation and the magic of transforming a body of photographs into a book with a life of its own.

_Interview with Publisher Gianluca Gamberini

Interview by Jim Casper_

[](javascript:;)

L’Artiere Edizioni: Photobooks as Collectible Art Objects

L’Artiere Edizioni’s Gianluca Gamberini talks about collaboration, experimentation and the magic of transforming a body of photographs into a book with a life of its own.

![Image 5: LArtiere Edizioni LArtiere Edizioni](https://www.lensculture.com/l-artiere-edizioni)

L’Artiere Edizioni is a photobook publishing company based in Bologna, Italy. It was founded in 2013 by twin brothers Gianluca and Gianmarco Gamberini. Coming from different, complementary disciplines (Gianluca made movies for 10 years, and Gianmarco had a background in production), they decided to join forces around an artistic medium that they both found fascinating — photobooks.

They got their start when their friend Larry Fink encouraged them to publish the European version of his book, \The Beat\_. They began to develop a series of photobooks, and Larry introduced the brothers to photographer Andrea Modica, whose work they continue to publish today. After a couple years learning the business of publishing and distribution, they continually moved in more and more experimental, conceptual directions for their book designs. Today l’Artiere is highly regarded worldwide as a creator of books that are like collectible works of art themselves.

We’re delighted that Gianluca has agreed to serve on the jury of the first LensCulture Photobook Prize. He spoke with LensCulture’s Jim Casper for this interview. Their conversation has been edited._

Jim Casper: Hi Gianluca. We’re so excited about this new Photobook Prize and really grateful that you’re going to be on the jury. You are known for creating very unique photobooks. Can you tell me a little bit about how you got started, and how you describe your company to people who don’t know it yet?

Gianluca Gamberini: It’s an honor. Thank you.

I think that in our DNA, there are a lot of ideas of experimental things.

After our first two years of publishing excellent traditional books, we wanted really to do something that was more into our idea of a photobook. With Larry’s book and books like the first book with Andrea Modica, we had this chance to start to understand the market and to make the connections with others in the book world. So that was amazing, but it was a little bit limited.

A spread from Larry Fink’s The Beats. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

So Gianmarco and I found that we both really loved this work of Amy Friend — Stardust. She won the Photolucida Award that year. When we saw the work we said, “Oh, I think we could do something different, something unique — in between an artist book and something for a larger public audience.”

And so with Gianmarco, we came up with this idea of interpreting her physical approach to working with archival images in a book. We used the laser to recreate the holes on the page. And then with French binding and very thin paper (like a Bible paper) when you turn the page, you have this impression of light passing through. And that was really like, “Okay! This is what we really like in book.”

From that moment on, we were always trying to treat every book like it was unique. We work with different designers. Every time at the beginning when we decide to work with a photographer, we try to think which designer is the best option for the photographer. And then together with the designer, we work with some idea or concept, and then little by little we create the book.

A fold-out cover for a book by Hitoshi Fugo. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

It sounds like you’re doing something that you’re really passionate about, and it seems like it makes you really happy on a personal level, too.

Very. Very. But I think that every publisher has the same feeling. Otherwise, we probably would do something else.

Yes. Tell me what kind of work seems to fit especially well with L’Artiere?

I think that sometimes it’s difficult to say, but basically we have to fall in love with the work. It has to have a strong sense of empathy for sure. We have to feel the empathy through the image. Sometimes I see that we are very connected also with stories about with connection with family or community. Not always, but that for sure. We really love long-term projects. But this is not always something that you can apply for every book. And also at the end, we need to be able to sell the book to the public. That’s also an important consideration.

A spread from Anders Petersen’s Napoli. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

After 13 years, do you feel you know when a book is going to sell? Do you feel pretty confident?

Gianmarco is better. I’m always confident. He’s better than me, I have to say, in predicting this. But we are 50-50. It’s a democracy, so we try.

It seems like it’s working well. For the LensCulture Photobook Prize, we’re asking photographers to submit 20 to 30 images and a short statement. Is that enough for you as a publisher to gauge whether something would be a good book?

I think that it’s enough to understand or at least to maybe say, “Oh, I want to see more. I want to know more.” It’s a good starting point. Sometimes when I receive an application, I ask photographers to send me a PDF with their own idea of sequence. Even if we will do something completely different, at least we see an intention. And sometimes also I ask if they have already a dummy, send me a video of the dummy even if, again, we will do something completely different. But at least I see something, an intention about it. But I think the 20 image is more than enough to ask. We also have to judge if something that is appropriate for a larger public, and I think the 20 image is great.

And how important is writing to you? A statement, a title, captions, essays — is that a big part of your books or would you say they are more picture and object-oriented?

I think that it is fundamental for a photographer to write about his work. I always ask every photographer to write a little statement about their work. Maybe we will not publish it, but I think it’s very important to have it for both them and for us to better understand the work. We tend to not have curatorial texts. If I have to add something, I prefer to have four or five lines from the photographer at the end at the colophon that is telling in his or her own words. They are photographers, they’re not writers. Nobody’s looking for a Nobel Prize. But I think that that’s the most important text that you can have in a photo book if you need to have it. And some works, of course, are so connected with a text, so of course you need to combine the image with the text.

Tragedia. Photography by Nicola Lo Calzo. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Tell me how you get your books out into the world.

Photo fairs are the greatest for us, even if it’s a lot of work. A fair offers a great way to show your book because at the end we all produce physical objects that you can only appreciate live. And that’s an incredible way of meeting your public. And then of course, as an independent publisher, we sell a lot online on our online store. Also our heroes are bookstores, and especially specialized bookstore around the world. In Europe, I think we have maybe a little bit more of very independent photo bookstores, but in US too, I think. And they are our first target for where to sell our books. We have several distributors: a US distributor and a European distributor, and a little Japanese distributor, who all help us also to sell copies to a larger public.

Our books are objects that become more and more elaborate and precious and the quantities are not so big that I think at one point the people who buy and sell our books are really very passionate about the books.

What does a photo book do that an exhibition or a website or a magazine feature can’t do? What makes a photo book different from those things?

My background is in movies. So for me, this is really a good question. An exhibition is in one moment in time. You create something on a wall, but you give a lot of freedom also to people to interpret it, the narrative. But a book, to me, there is a line and there is a narration. So to me, it’s much more connected to an idea of movie maybe. And also a book stays for a long time. A book doesn’t need electricity to switch on. The magic thing of a book is that when you produce a book, when you publish a book, the book has its own life, and then you never know who will be in touch with the book and how many people will pass the book from one to the other. So that’s also quite magical, I have to say.

Yes. Magical is the word for it. I have favorite books that feel like friends to me. I can take them off my bookshelf and suddenly I’m in a very happy space again. It’s really nice.

That’s exactly the happy space. I think that when you’re not feeling super great, you just spend some time with some photo books, and even if the topics are not maybe the most happy ones, they still give you hope.

Cover of Catholic Girls by Andrea Modica. Courtesy of L’Artiere Edizioni.[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/lartiere-edizioni-l-artiere-edizioni-photobooks-as-collectible-art-objects#)

Can you give any words of advice to photographers who want to make a photo book?

So first of all is really to do some research. There are many different publishers. It’s a fantastic moment for photo book publisher. We have many, many different ones. And each one of us has really his own particularity. And so I think that I know it’s difficult for a photographer to be very objective about this work, but I think you have to try to see which publisher could be a good fit for you. And maybe, even, don’t be obsessed in having a book that is produced by a publisher because sometime you can do it yourself, and today also is amazing for this. Sometime you can also do a self-publishing book, maybe doing 50 or 100 copies. And I don’t know, it’s just a different way of achieve your objective that is as good as going with a publisher, I think.

I think certainly an advantage of someone publishing a book with you is you have experience, you’re going to put together a book that’s going to be a beautiful object as well as it’s going to treat the photos with respect, but then you’re also going to get it out into the world. It’s not going to sit in someone’s garage because they don’t know how to distribute it. That’s a pretty big part of it, right?

That’s a big part, I have to say. Also, I have to say two other things. I think that not every photography work maybe has to be a book also. Now I think that everyone thinks that his or her work has to be a book. I don’t know. And second of all, I think that — and it’s very important for a photographer, working with a publisher to realize — that it’s really more similar to making a movie. There are many different people working together. Each one has his own idea. Even though photographers are really used to working all by themselves, doing a photo book is teamwork. It is a big collaboration. It’s not easy sometimes to, especially for photographer at their first photo book. It’s difficult sometime if they’re not used to working in team.

What’s your favorite part of the publishing process?

Meeting people. And I think that my favorite part is really when you see a work and you have the capacity to create something new and fresh with the work. That’s really the most magical part. When you see the potential and then you can make it rise above where it is right now.

Often, photographers will say, “Oh, thank you. And thank you to the designer. You allow me to see my work in a different way.” And that’s a great thing, I think.

Mi madre no trabaja: maternidad y trabajo invisible en imágenes

¿Qué significa «no trabajar» cuando los días se consumen manteniendo unidos a una familia y un hogar? Olga Steinepreis responde con ingenio, surrealismo y una cámara.

«Soy oficialmente ama de casa», dice Olga Steinepreis al presentar su nuevo proyecto. «Decirlo en voz alta todavía me avergüenza porque la palabra conlleva una sombra de ociosidad. Sin embargo, siempre hay trabajo esperando, ese tipo de labor que mantiene vivo un hogar y que, de alguna manera, parece "hacerse sola"». La casa en Mi madre no trabaja se convierte en el escenario de este ciclo invisible de trabajo, lleno de calcetines sucios, platos y montañas de juguetes de plástico que brotan por doquier. Una sola figura es responsable de domesticar este entorno frenético: Steinepreis, cuyo cuerpo aparece retratado trabajando en diversas escenas de labor doméstica.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

La fotografía fue una presencia temprana en el hogar mientras Steinepreis crecía. Su padre era un aficionado que revelaba e imprimía sus propias fotografías. «De niña, me fascinaba ver cómo una imagen aparecía lentamente en una hoja de papel en blanco dentro del cuarto oscuro», relata. «Se sentía casi como algo mágico». Años después, el poder casi mágico de la cámara para hacer visibles las cosas sigue siendo una característica definitoria de todos sus proyectos imaginativos. Desarrollada en paralelo al nacimiento de su primer hijo, su propia práctica como artista le ha permitido observar la evolución de su vida desde la distancia, traduciendo sus sentimientos en fotografías escenificadas que contienen las múltiples —y a menudo invisibles— facetas de la maternidad.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Steinepreis tomó la cámara por primera vez para detener el tiempo y documentar a la nueva persona que había traído al mundo, antes de empezar a usarla como una brújula para navegar de regreso hacia su propia identidad. «Muchas experiencias de la maternidad son difíciles de explicar con palabras porque contienen contradicciones: amor y agotamiento, alegría y soledad, plenitud y la sensación de perderse gradualmente a una misma», explica. Para expresar esto, la artista ha desarrollado un lenguaje visual impregnado de surrealismo y absurdo que está profundamente arraigado en esa miríada de emociones que experimenta en la realidad cotidiana.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

A la vez autorretrato y personaje interpretado, la figura que anima las imágenes de Steinepreis se transforma a través de sus proyectos. En otra serie, I’ve had a dream…, la artista es un ser camaleónico, estirado en diferentes direcciones con brazos y cabezas adicionales. Se multiplica a sí misma, con diferentes versiones de su ser enfrentándose entre sí. En Mi madre no trabaja, son los objetos los que se multiplican, ahogando el cuerpo sin rostro: tareas invisibles y no reconocidas que se acumulan con el tiempo hasta llegar al exceso.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

«Normalmente, mis proyectos comienzan con algo que se niega a dejarme en paz. Puede ser una frase que escucho por casualidad, una situación cotidiana, un sentimiento de incomodidad o una contradicción que no acabo de entender», dice Steinepreis. La idea recurrente de Mi madre no trabaja fue un fragmento de una conversación que escuchó entre su hijo y un amigo. Cuando le preguntaron a qué se dedicaba su madre, el hijo de la artista respondió: «Mi mamá no trabaja. Bueno, cocina, mantiene la casa limpia, pero no tiene un trabajo de verdad». El comentario inocente volvió a ella una y otra vez mientras realizaba sus tareas diarias en casa.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

«Un día, mientras clasificaba una montaña de ropa sucia antes de meterla en la lavadora, sentí el impulso de montar mi cámara y las luces y tomé una fotografía», explica. «Esa imagen nunca llegó a formar parte de la serie final, pero marcó el inicio del proyecto. Me dio el lenguaje visual que quería seguir explorando y abrió una conversación que me sentí obligada a mantener a través de la fotografía».

En escenas elaboradamente construidas, el cuerpo frenético de Steinepreis desaparece en el entorno que se le ha encomendado mantener en funcionamiento. Durante el proceso de trabajo, la labor artística y la doméstica se encuentran. «Antes incluso de empezar a disparar, a menudo tengo que preparar el día de una manera muy práctica. Cocino las comidas con antelación e intento liberarme de tantas responsabilidades domésticas como sea posible», afirma. «Cuando finalmente logro materializar la visión, se convierte en una tarea muy física. Muevo muebles, reorganizo objetos, compongo la escena por capas con cuidado deliberado y diseño la iluminación para reforzar la atmósfera. Es como montar un pequeño escenario teatral». Tanto humorística como inquietante, la versión dramatizada de la vida cotidiana que se representa aquí se siente más cercana a la realidad que el relato inmaculado de la maternidad que domina las redes sociales.

De la serie Mi madre no trabaja © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

«¿Estaré alguna vez a la altura de este ideal? ¿Quién estableció este estándar en primer lugar? El problema no es que existan estos momentos brillantes y hermosos; existen, sin duda. El problema surge cuando se convierten en la única narrativa aceptable de la maternidad», reflexiona la artista. «Hay tan poco espacio para conversaciones honestas sobre el agotamiento, la frustración, el trabajo invisible o la lenta erosión de las propias necesidades bajo el peso de las exigencias de los demás. El tiempo, la energía y la atención de una mujer se reorientan por completo hacia los otros. Incluso las pequeñas decisiones cotidianas —qué cocinar, cuándo descansar, cómo emplear su tiempo— se toman pensando en todos los demás. Gradualmente, ella puede empezar a desvanecerse de su propia historia».

A través de los proyectos que conforman su obra, Steinepreis va más allá de reescribirse en su propia historia para explorar una narrativa más colectiva. «No me interesa retratar la maternidad solo como lucha o sacrificio, del mismo modo que no me interesa presentarla como una alegría infinita».

My Mother Doesn’t Work: Motherhood and Invisible Labor in Pictures

What does it mean to “not work” when your days are consumed by keeping a family and household together? Olga Steinepreis answers with wit, surrealism and a camera.

_Photographs by Olga Steinepreis

Text by Sophie Wright_

[](javascript:;)

My Mother Doesn’t Work: Motherhood and Invisible Labor in Pictures

What does it mean to “not work” when your days are consumed by keeping a family and household together? Olga Steinepreis answers with wit, surrealism and a camera.

“I am officially a housewife,” says Olga Steinepreis introducing her new project. “Saying it out loud still embarrasses me because the word carries a shadow of idleness. Yet there is always work waiting, the kind that keeps a home alive and somehow appears to ‘do itself.’’’ The house in My Mother Doesn’t Work becomes a stage for this invisible cycle of work, full of dirty socks, dishes, erupting mountains of plastic toys. One sole figure is responsible for taming this frenzied environment—Steinepreis, whose body is pictured at work throughout various scenes of domestic labor.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Photography was an early presence at home while Steinepreis was growing up. Her father was an amateur who developed and printed his own photographs. “As a child, I was fascinated by watching an image slowly appear on a blank sheet of paper in the darkroom,” she recounts. “It felt almost magical.” Years later, the camera’s near-magical power to make things visible remains a defining feature of all of her imaginative projects. Unfolding in parallel with the birth of her first child, her own practice as an artist has allowed her to watch the evolution of her life from a distance, translating her feelings into staged photographs that hold the many—often invisible—facets of motherhood.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Steinepreis first picked up the camera to still time and document the new person she had brought into the world, before beginning to use it as a compass to navigate her way back to her own identity. “Many experiences of motherhood are difficult to explain with words because they contain contradictions: love and exhaustion, joy and loneliness, fulfilment and the feeling of gradually losing yourself,” she explains. To express this, the artist has developed a visual language steeped in surrealism and absurdity that is deeply rooted in this myriad of emotions she experiences in everyday reality.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

Both a self-portrait and a character that is being performed, the figure animating Steinepreis’ images morphs across projects. In another series, I’ve had a dream…, the artist is a shapeshifting being, stretched in different directions with extra arms and heads. She multiples herself, different selves staring each other down. In My Mother Doesn’t Work, it is things that multiply, drowning out the faceless body—invisible, unrecognized chores that rack up over time amassing to excess.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“Usually, my projects begin with something that refuses to leave me alone. It can be a sentence I overhear, an everyday situation, a feeling of discomfort, or a contradiction I don’t quite understand,” Steinepreis says. The earworm of My Mother Doesn’t Work was a snippet of conversation that she overheard during a conversation between her son and his friend. When asked what his mother did for a living, the artist’s son replied: “My mom doesn’t work. Well, she cooks, keeps the house clean, but she hasn’t got a real job.” The innocent remark returned to her again and again as she performed her daily chores at home.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“One day, while sorting a pile of laundry before putting it into the washing machine, I felt the urge to set up my camera and lights and took a photograph,” she explains. “That image never became part of the final series, but it marked the beginning of the project. It gave me the visual language I wanted to continue exploring and opened up a conversation I felt compelled to have through photography.”

In elaborately constructed scenes, Steinepreis’ frantic body disappears into the environment she has been tasked with keeping in working order. During the work process, artistic and domestic labor meet. “Before I can even begin shooting, I often have to prepare for the day in a very practical way. I cook meals in advance and try to free myself from as many household responsibilities as possible,” she says. “When I finally get to realize the vision, it becomes a very physical undertaking. I move furniture, rearrange objects, layer the scene with deliberate care, and craft the lighting to support the mood. It’s like staging a small theatre set.” Both humorous and upsetting, the dramatized version of everyday life that gets played here feels closer to reality than the pristine narrative of motherhood that dominates social media.

From the series, My Mother Doesn’t Work © Olga Steinepreis[](https://www.lensculture.com/articles/olga-steinepreis-my-mother-doesn-t-work-motherhood-and-invisible-labor-in-pictures#)

“Will I ever live up to this ideal? Who set this standard in the first place? The issue isn’t that these bright, beautiful moments exist—they absolutely do. The problem arises when they become the only acceptable narrative of motherhood,” the artist ponders. “There’s so little room for honest conversations about the exhaustion, the frustration, the invisible labor, or the slow erosion of one’s own needs beneath the weight of everyone else’s demands. A woman’s time, energy, and attention get reoriented entirely around others. Even small, everyday choices—what to cook, when to rest, how to spend her time—are made with everyone else in mind. Gradually, she can start to fade out of her own story.”

Across the projects that make up her body of work, Steinepreis goes beyond writing her way back into her own story to explore a more collective narrative. “I am not interested in portraying motherhood only as struggle or sacrifice, just as I am not interested in presenting it as endless joy.”

Cuando la vida vuelve a empezar a los 60: retratos lúdicos de ucranianos desplazados

A través del seguimiento de un grupo de ucranianos que huyeron de la guerra hacia Bratislava, esta colección de retratos equilibra la tristeza y el humor para explorar qué significa comenzar una nueva vida después de los 60 años.

_Fotografías de Maryna Syrovatka

Entrevista de Sophie Wright_

La práctica de Maryna Syrovatka aborda las transiciones: esos momentos en los que la vida se interrumpe, las estructuras familiares se disuelven y se reconstruyen de nuevo. Sus proyectos, y su propia vida, se han visto marcados por el desplazamiento causado por la invasión rusa de Ucrania y por las historias individuales de quienes tuvieron que dejarlo todo atrás. En Don’t Worry, I’m Fine, se reunió con recién llegados a su hogar de adopción en Eslovaquia. En su estudio, creó un espacio capaz de albergar emociones difíciles y contradicciones.

On Butterflies and Dinosaurs se centra en una etapa diferente del desplazamiento: ¿qué sucede cuando la vida debe empezar de nuevo a los 60 años? Siguiendo a hombres y mujeres ucranianos que ahora viven en Bratislava, su proyecto más reciente equilibra la tristeza y el humor mientras celebra la resiliencia de una comunidad de personas que se enfrentan al reto de recomenzar en un lugar nuevo, lejos de casa. En sus retratos lúdicos, Syrovatka crea espacio para la realidad paradójica de la supervivencia y las distintas formas en que esta generación ha encontrado para sobrellevar su situación.

En esta entrevista para LensCulture, Maryna Syrovatka conversa con Sophie Wright sobre la fotografía como diálogo, el proceso de trabajo tras sus imaginativas imágenes y la inspiración que encuentra en otra generación.

Sin título © Maryna Syrovatka

Sophie Wright: Comenzaste tu vida profesional como abogada. ¿Qué te alejó del derecho y te llevó a la fotografía?

Maryna Syrovatka: En realidad es difícil de responder porque no sucedió de la noche a la mañana. A lo largo de varios años, la vida a mi alrededor cambió: fui madre, perdí a mis padres, viví los acontecimientos que precedieron a la guerra en Ucrania y su inicio en 2014, y finalmente me mudé a otro país. Creo que cada uno de estos sucesos desempeñó su propio papel, pero, sinceramente, lo que finalmente me impulsó fue simplemente el deseo de intentarlo.

La fotografía ha estado presente en mi vida desde la infancia. Mis padres me enseñaron los conceptos básicos de la fotografía analógica en blanco y negro. Revelar carretes y hacer copias juntos me parecía algo mágico. Pero estaba convencida de que no era una persona creativa. En el sistema soviético, la educación artística parecía muy rígida: o sabías dibujar un jarrón o no sabías. Yo no sabía, así que ni siquiera me planteé un camino artístico. La fotografía seguía siendo una especie de fruto prohibido.

En aquel entonces, trabajaba como abogada en una gran firma internacional de servicios profesionales. Tenía experiencia, cualificaciones y una identidad profesional estable. La fotografía significaba volver a ser principiante. Recuerdo preguntarle a alguien: «¿Cómo sabes si este es el camino en el que realmente podrías destacar?». Me respondió: «Nunca se sabe. Nadie lo sabe». Fue una respuesta obvia, pero también un gran alivio. No hay garantías. Necesitaba escuchar eso y dejar de buscar una. Simplemente tienes que intentarlo. Creo que esa es también la belleza de la vida.

Ejercicios matutinos © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: ¿Ha influido de alguna manera tu pasado en la abogacía en tu práctica artística?

MS: Mucho más de lo que esperaba. El derecho y el arte tienen mucho más en común de lo que uno podría imaginar. Ambos implican interpretación y juicio, y ambos están llenos de complejidades. Un argumento legal tiene su propia forma, ritmo y marco. Cada palabra y cada detalle importan, e incluso un pequeño cambio puede alterar todo el significado.

Cuando ejerces el derecho, comprendes lo complejo que es el mundo y lo complejas que son las personas que lo habitan. Cuando me acerco a alguien a través de la fotografía, esa complejidad me atrae. Le da otra dimensión al trabajo. La práctica legal me entrenó para escuchar con atención, fijarme en los detalles y evitar sacar conclusiones precipitadas.

SW: El tema, o más bien la pregunta, que parece recorrer todos tus proyectos es qué sucede cuando la vida se interrumpe. Cómo la crisis altera tanto nuestro mundo exterior como el interior, y cómo nos reconstruimos. ¿Por qué dirías que la fotografía es el medio que has elegido para hablar de esto?

MS: Cuando algo sucede, ya sea un evento global o una ruptura personal, la persona se encuentra, en última instancia, muy sola en su experiencia. Siempre es algo más profundo y complicado de lo que parece desde fuera. Por ejemplo, tras la invasión a gran escala de Ucrania por parte de Rusia, millones de personas cruzaron hacia la Unión Europea. Pero la situación de cada individuo es un universo entero. Cada persona tiene que lidiar con los cambios en su vida a su manera.

Para mí, la fotografía no es solo una herramienta para tomar una imagen. Todo el proceso importa. Me brinda la oportunidad de conectar con alguien y, quizás, decirle: «Oye, te veo, y me importa lo que te está pasando». Escuchar es una parte muy importante, aunque invisible, de ese proceso.

Me encanta hablar con las personas a las que fotografío y conocer sus experiencias personales, incluso cuando lo que comparten es traumático. Este microcosmos me ofrece una perspectiva mucho mejor de los grandes acontecimientos, y una comprensión o sentimiento que puedo trasladar a la imagen.

Halyna de paseo © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: Has descrito el estudio de forma hermosa como un espacio para «albergar» momentos de incertidumbre y transición. ¿Puedes hablarme un poco de tu práctica en el estudio y su relación con los temas en los que te centras en tu trabajo?

MS: Abrí mi estudio en Bratislava en 2021, poco antes de la invasión a gran escala. Quería que se pareciera a los estudios de Kiev que tanto me gustaban: minimalista, pero también cálido y acogedor, no puramente técnico. Al entrar, sientes que has pasado a otro mundo. Todavía había restricciones por el COVID, pero también cierta esperanza de que la vida volviera a la normalidad. Planeaba empezar con fotografía de moda. Luego, todo se desarrolló de forma muy distinta.

Cuando comenzó la invasión a gran escala, la fotografía me pareció irrelevante al principio. Empecé a trabajar como voluntaria en la línea de ayuda SOS Ucrania-Eslovaquia, intentando organizar transporte, alojamiento, medicinas y otra asistencia urgente. Al final, me agoté. Comprendí que no podía ayudar a todo el mundo y que necesitaba volver a algo que supiera hacer y que pudiera mantener. Así fue como el estudio adquirió un propósito completamente diferente.

Don’t Worry, I’m Fine se convirtió en el primer proyecto que realicé allí. El estudio pasó a ser un territorio al que podía invitar a la gente. Fue una decisión intuitiva ofrecer retratos y sesiones de fotos familiares durante los primeros días de la invasión, y luego a lo largo de los meses y años siguientes. La idea no era solo preservar recuerdos, sino también ofrecer algo de consuelo y la posibilidad de hablar y ser escuchado. Pasé mucho más tiempo con cada participante de lo que pasaría en una sesión de fotos habitual. Sentía que estaba ocurriendo algo muy importante, y que estas imágenes e historias tendrían mucho más valor en el futuro que en aquel momento.

Trabajar en el estudio es completamente diferente a fotografiar a alguien en un alojamiento temporal, no solo en términos de la imagen resultante, sino también en cuanto a cómo se siente la persona durante el proceso. Para algunas de las personas que conocí en aquel entonces, estoy totalmente segura de que ser fotografiadas en su alojamiento temporal habría resultado doloroso o intrusivo. No quería eso.

En el estudio hablábamos, bebíamos té y hacíamos muchas fotografías. Para mí era importante no solo obtener algo del encuentro, sino también ofrecer algo a cambio. El estudio hizo posible este tipo particular de relación.

Halyna © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: ¿Cómo evolucionó este enfoque de estudio hacia On Butterflies and Dinosaurs? ¿Qué cambió en tu planteamiento?

MS: Ambos proyectos comenzaron en el estudio, pero se desarrollaron de forma muy distinta. Todos los participantes de Don’t Worry, I’m Fine fueron fotografiados allí. Intenté fotografiar en otros entornos, pero esas imágenes simplemente no funcionaban. Rompían la atmósfera y la cercanía particulares que se habían creado dentro del estudio. El estudio se convirtió en el lugar donde se registró esa cápsula del tiempo.

No puedo decir realmente que un proyecto evolucionara hacia el otro. De hecho, estaba en pleno proceso de publicación del libro y, sinceramente, dudaba de si volvería a embarcarme en un proyecto tan grande por mi cuenta. Pero, ¿qué otra cosa puedes hacer después de tener pensamientos así? Por supuesto, empezar otro proyecto.

On Butterflies and Dinosaurs también comenzó en el estudio. Nos reunimos, hablamos, grabamos las primeras entrevistas e hicimos retratos. Sin embargo, desde el principio, el trabajo fue más colorista, construido y lúdico. Desde el primer momento en que conocí a estas personas, supe que las fotografías serían en color. Muy pronto, el proyecto superó los límites del estudio. Mostrar a los participantes solo dentro de ese entorno restringido empezó a sentirse limitante. Para entonces, muchos de ellos ya formaban parte del paisaje de la ciudad. Tenían rutinas, actividades y relaciones en Eslovaquia, aunque su situación seguía sin resolverse.

Dinosaurios en invierno © Maryna Syrovatka

Otra diferencia importante es, sencillamente, el momento en que comenzaron los proyectos. Don’t Worry, I’m Fine empezó cuando la invasión a gran escala aún era reciente y la gente vivía el impacto inmediato, incluyéndome a mí. Realicé el proyecto porque sentía un fuerte impulso de hacerlo y creía que era importante. Pero también había tantas incertidumbres y emociones abrumadoras que hacían que el proceso fuera particularmente difícil.

Para 2024, sentí que habíamos alcanzado una especie de meseta. La gente empezaba a tomar decisiones: si regresar, si quedarse en el extranjero y cómo planificar una vida bajo condiciones que nadie había elegido. Para cuando empecé On Butterflies and Dinosaurs, ya estaban viviendo dentro de esta nueva realidad y procesándola de formas muy diversas. El proyecto necesitaba un lenguaje visual diferente y un espacio físico más amplio.

SW: ¿Qué te llevó a centrarte específicamente en el grupo de mayores de 60 años?

MS: Hay un grupo para personas mayores ucranianas en uno de los centros comunitarios de Bratislava, organizado por la ONG Sme Spolu (Estamos Juntos). Originalmente comenzó como una forma de apoyo psicológico, pero las primeras reuniones fueron difíciles. La gente estaba tan absorta en su propio duelo y pérdida que no necesariamente quería hablar o escuchar a los demás. Poco a poco, los voluntarios empezaron a ofrecer diferentes actividades: baile, pintura, marcha nórdica, ejercicios matutinos, ensayos de coro. El grupo acabó convirtiéndose en uno de los más activos. Se apuntaban a casi todo lo que se les ofrecía y empezaron a actuar en diferentes eventos.

Su energía me llamó la atención. Para ser sincera, esperaba encontrarme con personas que estuvieran simplemente devastadas. Piénsalo bien. Muchos de ellos nacieron durante o poco después de la Segunda Guerra Mundial. Vivieron la Unión Soviética, su colapso, la independencia de Ucrania...

When Life Begins Again at 60: Playful Portraits of Displaced Ukrainians

Following a group of Ukrainians who fled the war to Bratislava, this collection of portraits balance sadness and humor to explore what it’s like to start a new life over the age of 60.

_Photographs by Maryna Syrovatka

Interview by Sophie Wright_

Maryna Syrovatka’s practice deals with transitions—moments when one’s life becomes interrupted, familiar structures dissolved and rebuilt anew. Her projects, and own life, have been shaped by the displacement caused by Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, and the individual stories of the people who had to leave everything behind. In Don’t Worry, I’m Fine , she met with new arrivals in her adopted home of Slovakia. In her studio, she created a space where difficult emotions and contradictions could be held.

On Butterflies and Dinosaurs focuses on a different stage of displacement: what happens when life has to start again at 60? Following Ukrainian men and women who now live in Bratislava, her latest project balances sadness and humor as it celebrates the resilience of a community of people who find themselves facing the challenge of starting over in a new place far from home. In her playful portraits, Syrovatka creates room for the paradoxical reality of what survival looks like—and the different ways this generation have found to cope with their situation.

In this interview for LensCulture, Maryna Syrovatka talks to Sophie Wright about photography as conversation, the work process behind her imaginative images and getting inspired by another generation.

Untitled © Maryna Syrovatka

Sophie Wright: You started your professional life as a lawyer. What led you away from law and into photography?

Maryna Syrovatka: It is actually difficult to answer because it did not happen overnight. Over several years, life around me changed: I became a mother, lost my parents, lived through the events that preceded the war in Ukraine and its beginning in 2014, and eventually moved to another country. I think each of these events played its own role, but honestly, what finally pushed me was simply the urge to try.

Photography had been present in my life since childhood. My parents taught me the basics of analog black and white photography. Developing film and making prints together felt like magic. But I was convinced that I was not a creative person. In the Soviet system, art education seemed very straightforward: either you could draw a vase or you could not. I could not, so I never even considered an artistic path. Photography remained a kind of forbidden fruit.

At the time, I was working as a lawyer in a large international professional services firm. I had experience, qualifications and a stable professional identity. Photography meant becoming a beginner again. I remember asking someone, “How do you know if that’s the path you might actually be good at?” They replied, “You never know. No one knows.” It was such an obvious answer, but also a great relief. There is no guarantee. I needed to hear that and stop looking for one. You simply have to try. I think that is also the beauty of life.

Morning Excercises © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: Has your past legal practice shaped your artistic practice in any way?

MS: Much more than I expected. Law and art have far more in common than one might imagine. Both involve interpretation and judgement, and both are full of intricacies. A legal argument has its own shape, rhythm and frame. Every word and detail matters, and even a small shift can change the whole meaning.

When you practice law, you understand how complex the world is and how complex the people inhabiting it are. When I approach someone through photography, this complexity attracts me. It gives another dimension to the work. Legal practice trained me to listen carefully, pay attention to detail and avoid jumping to simple conclusions.

SW: The theme, or rather question, that seems to run through all your projects is what happens when life is disrupted. How crisis interrupts both our external and internal world, and how we rebuild. Why would you say photography is your chosen medium to speak about this?

MS: When something happens, whether it is a global event or a personal rupture, a person is ultimately very alone in their experience. It is always deeper and more complicated than it appears from the outside. For example, after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine, millions of people crossed into the European Union. But each person’s situation is a whole universe. Each person has to deal with the changes in their life in their own way.

For me, photography is not only a tool for taking a picture. The whole process matters. It gives me an opportunity to connect with someone and perhaps to say: hey, I see you, and I care about what is happening to you. Listening is a very important, though invisible, part of that process.

I love talking to the people I photograph and learning about their personal experiences, even when what they share is traumatic. This microcosm gives me a much better perspective on larger events, and an understanding or feeling that I can carry into the picture.

Halyna on a Walk © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: You’ve described the studio beautifully as a space to “hold” moments of uncertainty and transition. Can you tell me a bit about your studio practice and its relationship to the themes you focus on in your work?

MS: I opened my studio in Bratislava in 2021, shortly before the full-scale invasion. I wanted it to resemble the studio spaces in Kyiv that I loved: minimal, but also warm and comfortable, not purely technical. When you enter, you feel that you have stepped into another world. There were still COVID restrictions, but also some hope that life was returning to normal. I was planning to begin with fashion photography. Then everything developed very differently.

When the full-scale invasion began, photography initially felt irrelevant. I started volunteering on the Ukraine-Slovakia SOS help line, trying to arrange transport, accommodation, medicine and other urgent assistance. Eventually, I burned out. I understood that I could not help everyone and needed to return to something I knew how to do and could sustain. That was how the studio acquired a completely different purpose.

Don’t Worry, I’m Fine became the first project I made there. The studio became a territory to which I could invite people. It was an intuitive decision to offer portraits and family photoshoots during the first days of the full-scale invasion, and then throughout the following months and years. The idea was not only to preserve memories, but also to offer some comfort and a possibility to talk and be heard. I spent much more time with each participant than I would during a usual photoshoot. It felt as though something very important was happening, and that these images and stories would matter much more in the future than they did at that moment.

Working in the studio is completely different from photographing someone in temporary accommodation, not only in terms of the resulting image, but also in terms of how the person feels during the process. For some of the people I met at the time, I am absolutely certain that being photographed in their temporary accommodation would have felt painful or intrusive. I did not want that.

In the studio, we talked, drank tea and made many photographs. It was important for me not only to take something from the encounter, but also to offer something in return. The studio made this particular kind of relationship possible.

Halyna © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: How did this studio approach evolve into On Butterflies and Dinosaurs? What changed in your approach?

MS: Both projects began in the studio, but they developed very differently. Everyone in Don’t Worry, I’m Fine was photographed there. I did try photographing in other environments, but those images simply did not work. They disrupted the particular atmosphere and closeness that had developed inside the studio. The studio became the place where this time capsule was recorded.

I cannot really say that one project evolved into the other. In fact, I was in the middle of publishing the book and honestly doubting whether I would ever embark on such a large project on my own again. But what else can you do after having thoughts like that? Of course, start another project.

On Butterflies and Dinosaurs also began in the studio. We met, talked, recorded our first interviews and made portraits. From the beginning, however, the work was more colorful, constructed and playful. From the first moment I met these people, I knew the photographs would be colorful. Very soon, the project outgrew the studio. Showing the participants only within that restricted environment began to feel limiting. By then, many of them had become part of the city landscape. They had routines, activities and relationships in Slovakia, even though their situation remained unresolved.

Dinosaurs in Winter © Maryna Syrovatka

Another important difference is simply when the projects began. Don’t Worry, I’m Fine started when the full-scale invasion was still new and people were living through its immediate shock, including me. I was making the project because I had this strong urge to do it and felt it was important. But there were also so many uncertainties and overwhelming emotions that made the process particularly difficult.

By 2024, I felt we had reached a certain plateau. People were beginning to make decisions: whether to return, whether to remain abroad and how to plan a life under conditions no one had chosen. By the time I started On Butterflies and Dinosaurs, they were already living inside this new reality and processing it in very different ways. The project needed a different visual language and a broader physical space.

SW: What drew you to focus on the specific age group of over-60s?

MS: There is a group for Ukrainian seniors at one of the community centres in Bratislava, organised by the NGO Sme Spolu, or We Are Together. It originally began as a form of psychological support, but the first meetings were difficult. People were so absorbed in their own grief and loss that they did not necessarily want to speak or listen to one another. Gradually, volunteers began offering different activities: dancing, painting, Nordic walking, morning exercises, choir rehearsals. The group eventually became one of the most active. They joined almost everything they were offered and began performing at different events.

Their drive drew my attention. To be honest, I expected to meet people who were simply devastated. Just think about it. Many of them were born during or shortly after the Second World War. They lived through the Soviet Union, its collapse, Ukrainian independence, the economic crises of the 1990s, and many other changes. When their lives had finally begun to settle, they were forced to leave again. If you look at it, their lives seem to fall between two wars.

Someone had to Knit the Sky © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: Tell me more about this mix of sadness and humour you’ve spoken about.

MS: The sadness is already built into the situation. The war has entered our lives on every level. Even though I live in safety, everything has changed permanently. While I was drafting these answers, six ballistic missiles struck the neighbourhood where close friends of mine live and where my family used to live. I closed my computer and started messaging everyone to ask whether they were safe. That is our new normal.

But this does not mean that everything has become grey. Often, it is the opposite. The background may be dark, but life remains extremely vivid. The humor and irony were not something I imposed on the project. They were already there, and they were also connected to social expectations about how displaced people should feel or behave.

I remember one photoshoot by a swimming pool. One of the women asked, half-jokingly, “What will people say? That we are having fun here and taking advantage of social support?” That sentence stayed with me. It revealed the burden of those expectations. Having fun can be seen as inappropriate, yet at the same time joy is attributed to you simply because you are now in safety. This paradox exists in both Western and Ukrainian society.

Neighborhood Watch © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: How did you meet the people you worked with? As someone of a younger generation, did you feel like you picked up any wisdom through the process of collaborating?

MS: Most of the participants belong to the senior club I mentioned, or are connected with it through friends and acquaintances.

My mother always wished my late grandmother would dress up, do her hair and make-up, and go out for coffee with friends. But during the last 10 years of her life, she hardly went out at all. I think this was partly connected to a very Soviet idea of ageing: once you get older, you should behave according to your age and gradually withdraw from life. It is not a very motivating model. It is actually quite a frightening one. And I know many people in Ukraine still follow this pattern.

So when I met this group, their energy was something I actually needed. When you meet an 82-year-old woman who walks 10,000 steps every day, wears short dresses and performs several dances in a row onstage, it changes your perspective. It reminds you that life does not end at 30, 40, 50 or 80, even when something as terrible as war has interrupted its ordinary course.

It has also been educational in a rather amusing way. I realized that many of the archetypes I associated with the older Soviet generation no longer described the people in front of me. I approached them with my own stereotypes and, to my amusement, those stereotypes turned out to be mine, not theirs.

This is one of the reasons I enjoy working with them. I can rarely predict how they will respond. They can be playful, stubborn, stylish, ironic, difficult, curious or very direct. I admire their appetite for life, but I do not want to turn that into another simplified image of universal strength or heroism.

Anti-Fragility © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: There is brightness and a childlike sense of play to your portraits that offers a striking contrast to the stories of displacement the people in them must have lived through. Can you tell me more about how you arrived at this colorful universe?

MS: My first impulse was to search for a shared coping mechanism, some secret of strength belonging to this generation. Very soon, that idea collapsed. I was meeting very different, vivid people, and any attempt to find one common feature would have simplified them.

At first, I considered following them through their everyday routines and working in a more documentary way. But after some time, I understood that this was not enough. The photographs reflected the sadness already built into the situation, but left very little space for the irony and contradictions that emerged through the process.

Their reality is paradoxical. They escaped a war and arrived in safety, but no one could have imagined finding themselves in this situation late in life. This new reality can feel almost dreamlike and absurd. Color, staging and handmade elements allowed me to bring that contradiction into the photographs and create a slight shift from ordinary reality. Some of the absurdity probably also comes from the dark sense of humor Ukrainians have developed during the years of the full-scale invasion. The ability to laugh even in the hardest circumstances can become a way of coping with something that otherwise feels impossible.

Flight Expectancy © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: Each image tells its own story. What was the work process like behind each picture? Did your subjects contribute to the idea?

MS: We began in the studio, with conversations. I needed time to get to know the people. Taken together, their stories became the basis for many of the ideas, but not in a literal way.

I did not want to illustrate what I had heard. I was more interested in the impressions these stories left with me and in translating them into a slightly displaced, sometimes almost dystopian visual reality. For example, the photograph of the two women knitting grew out of conversations with participants from Kramatorsk and Nikopol, two cities that have been heavily shelled since the beginning of the full-scale invasion. I had the image in my head for a very long time. I also had to knit the large carpet myself. It is quite big.

Usually, I arrive with a core, quite detailed idea. But once we begin, the participants are very active and bring their own responses. We usually make much more than I originally planned, which makes the final selection very difficult.

Mrs. Nadia’s Answer to Putin © Maryna Syrovatka

SW: Can you tell me about the photo Mrs. Nadia’s Answer to Putin?

MS: Mrs Nadia is a very creative person. She paints often and likes finding forms and resemblances in nature: in trees, clouds and especially stones. She frequently paints on the stones she finds, giving them another identity or perspective.

When she found this particular stone, it immediately resonated with her. She saw it as a gesture of defiance: “You won’t get me, Putin!” Whenever she feels sad, looking at the work makes her feel better. She has made other small works in response to the actions, and inaction, of political leaders. We later made a short reel in which she explains the work herself.

SW: And finally, how did you come up with the title?

MS: I had many working titles, but they all felt so flat, to be honest. Then one of the women came to the studio wearing a T-shirt that said “Stylish Butterflies.” She told me she had been a member of a senior club back in Ukraine. They did not want to call themselves grannies, so they chose “Butterflies” instead.

I loved it immediately. It was such a beautiful metaphor: fragility, beauty, fleeting moments. I knew butterflies had to be in the title, but I still could not find another word to balance it. Later, I was interviewing a couple and asked which stereotypes about their generation irritated them. The husband replied, “It’s very annoying that everyone sees us as dinosaurs.”

That was it: butterflies and dinosaurs. Afterwards, I knitted the dinosaur hats, and made these butterfly wings.

Estado de negación

Exiliada política de Bielorrusia, Sasha Velichko utiliza una inquietante fotografía de puesta en escena y visuales generados por IA para narrar las historias sepultadas de la violencia cotidiana ejercida por la dictadura de su país de origen.

_Fotografías de Sasha Velichko

Texto de Sophie Wright_

Estado de negación

Bailar y cantar, reunirse para tomar una taza de té, hablar en la lengua materna. En Bielorrusia, comúnmente calificada como la «última dictadura» de Europa, estos sencillos actos cotidianos pueden convertir a cualquiera en un criminal. Incluso rezar por la paz, un gesto realizado por un conocido cirujano vascular en la ciudad de Grodno un día de septiembre de 2020, terminó en un juicio.

01.09.2020 Detención por rezar © Sasha Velichko

En *Estado de negación*, de Sasha Velichko, este relato es rescatado del olvido mediante un breve texto acompañado de una imagen escenificada: la nuca de un hombre, cubierta de pequeñas cruces blancas. Frente a ella, una cuadrícula de 12 imágenes muestra las «noticias» difundidas por los medios estatales el mismo día del incidente. «El otoño huele a manzanas del jardín de la abuela», reza el pie de foto bajo una imagen de lo que parece ser una extremidad humana fundiéndose con unas frutas similares a manzanas verdes.

El otoño huele a manzanas del jardín de la abuela © Sasha Velichko

El anuncio de un nuevo curso escolar, ilustrado por una foto de grupo con rostros gesticulantes y derretidos. Una acusación de que la ONU ha publicado una noticia falsa, acompañada de la imagen de una antena parabólica deformada. Ambos conjuntos de imágenes visibilizan incidentes violentos de detención, al tiempo que llaman la atención sobre la forma en que el Estado oculta sus crímenes inundando el panorama mediático.

Aquí queda al descubierto el absurdo de la vida cotidiana bajo la represión estatal. Velichko —ella misma refugiada política, actualmente radicada en Polonia— realizó este trabajo en el exilio, observando desde fuera la maquinaria propagandística que opera en su país natal. Con formación en radiofísica, su sintonía con los métodos analíticos, los patrones y los sistemas nutre la forma de *Estado de negación*. La interacción entre la cuadrícula y la imagen individual refleja los mecanismos de los medios digitales y su siniestra capacidad para dirigir nuestro enfoque. «En la sociedad contemporánea, saturada de innumerables distracciones que compiten por nuestra atención, se ha vuelto habitual desviar la mirada de las imágenes que evocan malestar», explica la artista en su declaración.

21.04.2021 Detención por el idioma bielorruso © Sasha Velichko

«Los medios controlados por el gobierno ocultan información sobre el creciente número de detenidos políticos, la alarmante tasa de desapariciones y el papel de la constitución en la salvaguarda de los derechos individuales», afirma. Al sacar a la luz estas alarmantes historias de represión, las imágenes escenificadas de Velichko mezclan una sobreexposición onírica con la estética de la evidencia para crear escenas inquietantes que subrayan el comportamiento disparatado del gobierno.

La regla de las tres palabras principales: trabajadores, forraje, vacas. © Sasha Velichko

La cuadrícula de imágenes de la derecha emplea una estética igualmente pesadillesca: han sido generadas por IA. «Surgieron numerosos artículos de noticias irrelevantes y peculiares que coincidían con las fechas de los arrestos», explica Velichko. «Para cada caso, seleccioné 12 titulares publicados el día de la detención, para mostrar cómo, en momentos de crisis, la propaganda genera ruido visual e informativo». Un torrente de imágenes desconectadas de la realidad, basadas en ficciones presentadas como hechos, dialoga con las audaces imágenes de ficción de la artista, arraigadas en una verdad perturbadora. La combinación es necesariamente confusa, lo que da vida a la incertidumbre de vivir en la Bielorrusia actual.

16.09.2020 Detención por una reunión para tomar el té en el patio © Sasha Velichko

La reconfiguración que hace Velichko de un paisaje mediático —uno que reescribe la realidad para convertir actos ordinarios en delitos— revela la violencia que habitualmente intenta ocultar. Como espectadores, nos guía para mirar más allá del espectáculo del ruido superficial y enfrentarnos directamente a los inimaginables actos de opresión que son rasgos rutinarios del régimen.

Sasha Velichko

State of Denial

A political exile from Belarus, Sasha Velichko uses uncanny staged photography and AI-generated visuals to tell the buried stories of everyday violence enacted by the dictatorship of her home country.

_Photographs by Sasha Velichko

Text by Sophie Wright_

State of Denial

Dancing and singing, gathering together for a cup of tea, speaking in one’s mother tongue. In Belarus, commonly referred to as Europe’s “last dictatorship,” these gentle daily acts may have you down as a criminal. Even praying for peace, a gesture enacted by a well-known vascular surgeon in the city of Grodno one day in September 2020, ended in a trial.

01.09.2020 Detention for praying © Sasha Velichko

In Sasha Velichko’s State of Denial, this story is salvaged from oblivion in a short text accompanied by a staged image: the back of a man’s head, covered in small white crosses. Across from it, a grid of 12 images display the ‘news’ stories shown in state media the same day as the incident. “Autumn smells like apples from Granny’s garden,” a caption under an image of what looks like a human limb melting into some green apple-like fruit.

Autumn smells of apples from grandmother’s garden © Sasha Velichko

The announcement of a new school term, illustrated by a group photo of grimacing, melting faces. An accusation that the UN has posted a fake news story, paired with a picture of a warped satellite dish. The two sets of images make visible violent incidents of detention while drawing attention to the way the state hides their crimes by flooding the media landscape.

Here the absurdity of everyday life under state repression is laid bare. Velichko—a political refugee herself, now based in Poland—made this work in exile, looking at the propaganda machine at work in her home country from the outside. With a background in radiophysics, her attunement to analytical methods, patterns and systems feeds into the form of State of Denial. The interplay between the grid and the standalone image mirrors the mechanisms of digital media and its sinister ability to direct our focus. “In contemporary society, which is filled with countless distractions vying for our attention, it has become commonplace to avert our gaze from images that evoke discomfort,” the artist explains in her statement.

21.04.2021 Detention for the Belarusian language © Sasha Velichko

“The government-controlled media conceals information regarding the increasing count of political detainees, the alarming rate of disappearances and the constitution in safeguarding the rights of individuals,” she says. Bringing these alarming stories of repression to light, Velichko’s staged images mix a dreamlike overexposure with the aesthetics of evidence to create uncanny scenes that underline the nonsensical behavior of the government.

The rule of three main words - workers, fodder, cows. © Sasha Velichko

The grid of images on the right harness an equally-nightmarish aesthetics—they are generated by AI. “Numerous irrelevant and peculiar news articles emerged coinciding with the dates of arrests,” Velichko explains. “For each case, I selected 12 headlines published on the day of the arrest—to show how, in moments of crisis, propaganda generates visual and informational noise.” A flood of images untethered to reality, grounded in fiction presented as facts speak with the artist’s bold, fictional images rooted in unsettling truth. The combination is a necessarily confusing one which animates the uncertainty of living in Belarus today.

16.09.2020 Detention for tea gathering in the courtyard © Sasha Velichko

Velichko’s reconfiguration of a media landscape—one that rewrites reality to turn ordinary acts into crime—reveals the violence it usually tries to hide. As an audience, she guides us to look past the spectacle of surface noise and right in the face of the unimaginable acts of oppression that are routine features of the regime.

A lo largo del río Lea

A lo largo del East London’s River Lea, que fue una vez una vibrante arteria industrial, Mattia Corato traza un paisaje donde la naturaleza salvaje, la historia urbana y formas poco convencionales de vivir convergen tranquilamente.

Fotografías y textos de Mattia Corato

A lo largo del río Lea

Históricamente el río Lea ha desempeñado un papel importante en la configuración del desarrollo del paisaje urbano de East London. Durante la revolución industrial, fue una arteria vital para el transporte de carbón y materias primas en la ciudad. Hoy, la zona alrededor del río se ha transformado en un espacio recreativo creando una erupción verde inesperada en el corazón de la ciudad.

Cuando me mudé a Clapton hace unos años, no sabía mucho sobre el río Lea y los prados y bosques circundantes. Empecé a recorrer las vías fluviales y descubrí una naturaleza profundamente urbana, agitada con rastros humanos y espacios de sobrecrecimiento.

Edmonton © Mattia Corato

La comunidad de personas que viven a lo largo de las orillas del río representa una parte vibrante de la identidad moderna del río. Algunos se sienten atraídos por la libertad de vida en el agua, mientras que otros buscan una vida asequible en un área donde los costes de vivienda están aumentando.

El río refleja la diversidad cultural y el carácter distintivo de los barrios del este de Londres a través de los cuales fluye. Representa una escapada pacífica y preciosa de la vida de la ciudad gris y rápida. Un lugar donde el ritmo de la naturaleza se mezcla con la vida humana.

- Mattia Corato

Along the River Lea

Along East London’s River Lea, which was once a vibrant industrial artery, Mattia Corato traces a landscape where wild nature, urban history and unconventional ways of living quietly converge.

Photographs and text by Mattia Corato

Along the River Lea

Historically the River Lea has played an important role in shaping the development of East London’s urban landscape. During the industrial revolution, it was a vital artery for transporting coal and raw materials into the city. Today, the area around the river has transformed into a recreational space creating an unexpected green eruption in the heart of the city.

When I moved to Clapton few years ago, I did not know much about the River Lea and the surrounding meadows and woods. I started to cycle along the waterways and I discovered a deeply urban nature, dotted with human traces and overgrown spaces.

Edmonton © Mattia Corato

The community of people that live along the riverbanks represents a vibrant part of the river’s modern identity. Some are drawn to the freedom of life on the water, while others seek affordable living in an area where housing costs are rising.

The river mirrors the cultural diversity and distinctive character of the neighborhoods of East London through which it flows. It represents a peaceful and precious escape from the grey and fast city life. A place where the rhythm of nature blends with human life.
